transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-03 14:30 PDT
Duration: ~78 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Chen (Redwood SE), Laura Gomez (Nimbus CTO), Ravi Singh (Nimbus SRE), Mei Tan (Nimbus MLOps)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough): discuss scheduler knobs around max_num_seqs and token ceilings to handle bursty traffic, KV prefetch tradeoffs for cold vs warm caches, and how hybrid routing to Dedicated pools + on-prem fallback behaves during sustained peaks. Plan: run a joint benchmark and adjust token ceilings, provide config samples.

[00:00:00] Maya (AE): All right everyone, thanks for carving out the time. Quick intros then Ethan will drive the deep dive.
[00:00:08] Laura (CTO): Hi, Laura here. Appreciate it. We're trying to nail predictable throughput for our real-time triage assistant.
[00:00:12] Ethan (SE): Hey team, Ethan. I'll focus on the runtime knobs we typically tune — continuous batching, max_num_seqs, token limits, and some KV prefetch recommendations especially for VPC/on-prem deployments.
[00:00:25] Ravi (SRE): Great. We're mostly concerned about tail latency during morning batch spikes, and how to fall back to Dedicated or on-prem without tearing the SLA.
[00:00:35] Ethan (SE): Exactly. Quick note: some terminology may sound like our internal names — e.g., token_guard, slot_size, prefetch_window — those map to knobs in the scheduler.yaml.

[00:01:12] Ethan (SE): Let's start with the workload shape you described. Laura, you mentioned 5–10x RPS bursts around 9am and 2pm for 10–15 minutes, and long tail of small single-turn requests the rest of the day?
[00:01:22] Laura (CTO): Exactly. And 60% of those spikes are multi-turn transcripts pulled from our clinical queue — so sequence lengths vary. We also have privacy constraints — on-prem for PHI, VPC for non-PHI.

[00:02:10] Ethan (SE): Okay. For mixed sequence lengths the main levers are: continuous batching window (we call it batching_max_delay), max_num_seqs (max concurrent seqs per slot), token_ceiling per request, and KV cache prefetch settings.
[00:02:25] Ethan (SE): Continuous batching helps pump throughput when there are many short requests; but it can add tail latency to some long requests if max_num_seqs is too low.
[00:02:40] Ravi (SRE): Can you give numbers we should start from? We need concrete defaults.

[00:03:05] Ethan (SE): Sure — conservative starting points we've used in similar customers: batching_max_delay=12ms, slot_size=64 tokens, max_num_seqs=32 for normal usage. For burst profiles, bump max_num_seqs to 48 and increase slot_size to 80, but only if KV hit-rate is high — otherwise you'll pay for wasted compute on padded sequences.
[00:03:30] Mei (MLOps): When you say 'padded sequences' — do you mean sequence packing overhead on GPU?
[00:03:36] Ethan (SE): Yes — packing tries to group sequences to fill matrix dims. If sequences are widely different lengths, that packing inefficiency increases FLOPs. So for variable seq workloads we prefer smaller max_num_seqs and more aggressive prefetch to warm the KV cache.

[00:04:10] Laura (CTO): What's the KV prefetch story for on-prem? We saw cold cache stalls in our PoC last quarter.
[00:04:20] Ethan (SE): On-prem cold cache stalls are common. We recommend a two-pronged approach: proactive prefetch profiles tied to routing (when hybrid routing detects traffic trending to on-prem, spin up a small warmup job that prefetches the top N prefixes using your typical prompt sets), and opportunistic background prefetch when GPUs are idle. The prefetch_window determines how many tokens/prefixes we'll prefill.
[00:04:50] Ravi (SRE): How much overhead does prefetch add? We're worried about it stealing capacity during real spikes.
[00:04:58] Ethan (SE): Good point. Prefetch runs at low priority and is throttled by the scheduler — we set a prefetch_budget per-node, default 5% of GPU cycles. During sustained spikes it backs off automatically. For very tight SLAs you can disable prefetch and only do explicit warmup runs before traffic windows.

[00:05:40] Ethan (SE): Another pattern is hybrid routing with burst capacity: route to Hosted (Redwood API hosted) for immediate short bursts while provisioning Dedicated or on-prem for sustained load. We support automatic fallback but you control the policy — e.g., route to hosted for requests under 256 tokens and to Dedicated for longer sequences to optimize cost/latency.
[00:06:00] Laura (CTO): We need to keep PHI on-prem — so can't route PHI to hosted. Any recommendations for that gating logic?
[00:06:10] Maya (AE): We usually gate by a data tag in the request. Our SDK supports a metadata header like x-redwood-data-class and the router policy can be written to strictly send PHI to Private deployment.

[00:06:40] Ethan (SE): Back to knobs: token_ceiling is important. If you set a per-request token_cap that's too high, the scheduler might let a very long request consume many tokens in a slot, causing head-of-line blocking. We often enforce token_ceiling=1024 for mixed workloads and enforce streamable generation for longer outputs to reduce slot time.
[00:07:05] Ravi (SRE): And max_num_seqs reduces head-of-line blocking?
[00:07:08] Ethan (SE): Indirectly. max_num_seqs limits how many sequences can be coalesced in a single kernel invocation. Lowering it reduces time each batch holds kernels, but can reduce batching efficiency. It's a tradeoff. For latency-sensitive small requests drop max_num_seqs to 16; for throughput-sensitive bulk set to 48+.

[00:08:00] Mei (MLOps): What about quantization effects? Our on-prem nodes are int8/blk8 capable. Does quant help latency enough to change these knobs?
[00:08:10] Ethan (SE): Quantization (int8/int4) usually reduces per-token execution time and memory, which improves throughput but can affect KV cache hit packing if kv keys are model-dependent. For a given model, if quantized runs 20–30% faster, you can tighten token ceilings or increase max_num_seqs without exceeding latency SLOs. But we recommend running short A/B for quality — some models show minor quality drift.

[00:08:50] Laura (CTO): We need to validate quality for clinical prompts; can Redwood help with eval runs?
[00:08:55] Maya (AE): Yes, we can run evals and share a template eval harness — we also have Redwood Optimize suggestions for quant profiles.

[00:09:30] Ethan (SE): Let's walk through a sample scheduler profile for your case. I'll read a condensed version and then paste the full YAML after the call.
[00:09:38] Ethan (SE): [reads] scheduler.yaml: default_route: private, burst_route: hosted, batching_max_delay: 12ms, slot_size: 80, max_num_seqs: 40, token_ceiling: 1024, prefetch_window: 128 prefixes, prefetch_budget: 5%, token_guard: enabled, fallback_policy: canary->hosted.
[00:10:02] Ravi (SRE): That max_num_seqs=40 seems high given our variable sequences. What if we experience long sequences that block?
[00:10:12] Ethan (SE): Good question. We set token_guard which prevents a single sequence from exceeding token_ceiling per slot. Also the scheduler supports sequence priority — short interactive requests get priority to reduce latency.

[00:11:00] Mei (MLOps): How do we measure if prefetch is actually improving hit-rate? Do you provide metrics?
[00:11:06] Ethan (SE): Yes, Console exposes KV hit-rate at per-model and per-node granularity, plus prefetch success rate and time-to-warm. We also expose a metric for eviction churn. You can set alerts when hit-rate drops below X% during windows.

[00:12:20] Laura (CTO): We have strict audit requirements; if any hooks prefetch PHI data how is it logged?
[00:12:30] Maya (AE): Prefetch only uses anonymized prefix tokens from your training prompt sets if provided. All prefetch activity is logged; we can route logs to your SIEM in the VPC/private setup and it respects KMS keys.

[00:13:10] Ethan (SE): Another real-world trick: use a small burst-only slot with very small slot_size and low max_num_seqs to serve short bursts with low tail latency — call it 'fast lane'. The scheduler can detect short requests and route them to the fast lane temporarily. That preserves capacity in the main lanes for long-running seqs.
[00:13:40] Ravi (SRE): Interesting — is that automatic or do we need to maintain two pools?
[00:13:45] Ethan (SE): You can do either. Hosted customers can use auto-provisioned fast lanes. For Dedicated/on-prem, we recommend a reserved small pool (2–4 GPUs) as fast lane. We include autoscaler policies that keep that pool warm.

[00:14:30] Laura (CTO): During a 10–15 minute spike in the morning, is it better to burst into Hosted for the excess or scale on-prem?
[00:14:40] Ethan (SE): If PHI routing prevents Hosted, you must scale on-prem. If you can route non-PHI, we recommend hybrid: route non-PHI to Hosted immediately (lower latency), while on-prem scales up for PHI. The cost tradeoff depends on frequency of spikes — Hosted cost per token is higher but gives instant elasticity.

[00:15:12] Maya (AE): We saw a question in chat about cold restart behavior for large models when new nodes come up — how does KV prefetch interplay?
[00:15:21] Ethan (SE): When nodes start from cold, the first few requests pay a kernel load and kv misses. Prefetch helps by priming the KV caches with common prefix tokens. Also we recommend a warmup job that issues a set of representative prompts at low priority as soon as nodes become available.

[00:16:05] Ravi (SRE): For our benchmark, what metrics should we capture?
[00:16:09] Ethan (SE): At minimum: p50/p90/p95/p99 latency for generations, tokens/sec, KV hit-rate, GPU utilization, eviction churn, batching efficiency (avg batch fill), and cold-cache time-to-warm. Also track cost per 1k tokens if comparing Hosted vs Dedicated.

[00:17:00] Mei (MLOps): If we enable int4 quant on on-prem, any special considerations for KV cache format?
[00:17:08] Ethan (SE): KV caches are largely format-agnostic but some lower-precision kernels require different packing. We'll provide the quantization profile that ensures compatibility and a quick verification script.

[00:18:30] Laura (CTO): What are common failure modes when tuning these knobs?
[00:18:36] Ethan (SE): Top ones: (1) increasing max_num_seqs without enough KV hit-rate — causes wasted compute and higher latency, (2) aggressive prefetch_budget stealing cycles during unexpected load, (3) token_ceiling set too high causing head-of-line blocking, (4) forgetting to tag PHI leading to routing mistakes.

[00:19:40] Ravi (SRE): Can Redwood automatically revert to safer defaults if we misconfigure?
[00:19:45] Ethan (SE): Yes — we have safety guards and an automatic fallback policy. If latency or error rates exceed thresholds, the router will divert new traffic to Hosted or a backup pool depending on policy.

[00:20:30] Maya (AE): Let's sketch the benchmark plan — Ethan?
[00:20:34] Ethan (SE): Proposed: 48 hour benchmark in three phases — phase A: 24h baseline with normal knob set (max_num_seqs=32, prefetch_budget=5%), phase B: 12h burst simulation with scheduled spikes (x10 RPS for 15m every hour) testing fast-lane + hosted fallback, phase C: 12h cold-cache recovery test with node restarts and prefetch profiles on. We'll collect the metrics I listed and produce a joint report.

[00:21:20] Laura (CTO): Sounds reasonable. We'll provide real prompt sets and the privacy tags so you can simulate PHI-safe routing.
[00:21:26] Ethan (SE): Great — we'll also include a short guide on tuning cost vs latency — e.g., how quant + higher batching can reduce token cost by 30% but may slightly increase variance in tail latency.

[00:22:10] Ravi (SRE): For the initial test bed, what node spec do you recommend?
[00:22:15] Ethan (SE): For on-prem, 80GB A100 or equivalent; if you're on 48GB hardware we'll provide smaller batch heuristics. For very large models you need multi-GPU sharding which changes the scheduler settings slightly.

[00:23:00] Mei (MLOps): Can we get a suggested YAML and a runbook for rollback?
[00:23:05] Maya (AE): Yes, we'll attach both. Ethan will include the YAML; I'll include the runbook and compliance attachments.

[00:24:00] [brief silence, background noise: keyboard clacks]

[00:24:30] Laura (CTO): One more question — SLA expectations if we use hybrid routing with Hosted for non-PHI: any cold-starts from Hosted side when you suddenly jump traffic?
[00:24:38] Ethan (SE): Hosted has fast cold-starts for small models; for large ones we do a warm-pool for burst handling. We'll provide expected p95 numbers for hosted bursts in the docs we send.

[00:25:10] Maya (AE): Anything else from the Nimbus team?
[00:25:14] Ravi (SRE): No, that's it for now. We'll confirm test nodes and calendar invites.
[00:25:20] Laura (CTO): Thanks — this was useful.

[00:25:30] Ethan (SE): Okay wrapping up — recap of next steps: Ethan sends scheduler.yaml & prefetch profile, Maya sends SOC2/KMS notes, Nimbus provisions nodes. We'll schedule the kickoff session.

[00:25:50] Maya (AE): Thanks all.

[00:26:00] -- End of main discussion; rest of meeting 45m was Q&A and granular config walkthrough --
[00:26:05] [00:26:05] Ethan (SE): Going deeper — here's an example of throttling expression for token_guard: if (request.tokens_in_slot + request.expected_tokens) > token_ceiling then mark as chunked and stream. This prevents single requests from monopolizing a slot.
[00:27:10] Ravi (SRE): In practice how do we compute expected_tokens? We have variable text gen.
[00:27:15] Ethan (SE): We estimate with a lightweight predictor using historical average length per prompt type — the scheduler accepts a hint from the SDK. If hint missing, it uses conservative default.
[00:28:20] Mei (MLOps): Our SDK is in Go — is there a sample for hint header?
[00:28:24] Ethan (SE): Yes, header x-redwood-expected-tokens: 120. We'll provide client snippets.
[00:30:00] [00:30:00] Ethan (SE): Now about eviction churn — if prefetch_window is too large on limited memory GPUs you see frequent evictions; that increases KV miss rate. We typically set prefetch_window to 128 prefixes for 80GB class, and 64 for 48GB class.
[00:32:10] Ravi (SRE): If eviction churn is high, is there any adaptive algorithm?
[00:32:16] Ethan (SE): Yes we have an adaptive prefetch throttle that reduces prefetch budget and shrinks window based on eviction events. We'll include telemetry so you can monitor churn and let the adaptive control run.
[00:34:00] [lots of configuration questions back and forth — abbreviated]

[00:42:20] [00:42:20] Laura (CTO): So to be explicit: what initial config will Redwood test with us during the benchmark?
[00:42:28] Ethan (SE): We'll test three configs: conservative (max_num_seqs=24, slot_size=64, prefetch_budget=2%), balanced (max_num_seqs=32, slot_size=72, prefetch_budget=5%), and aggressive (max_num_seqs=48, slot_size=96, prefetch_budget=8%) with and without int8 quant.

[00:45:00] Ravi (SRE): Any suggested alert thresholds?
[00:45:05] Ethan (SE): p95 latency > 450ms during normal periods, or KV hit-rate < 60% — trigger an alert. During bursts you can relax p95 to 900ms depending on SLA.

[00:50:00] [00:50:00] Maya (AE): I'm going to start closing this out — Ethan will prepare the config pack and we'll send it.
[00:50:08] Ethan (SE): I'll also attach the small verification script for quant checks.
[00:50:15] Laura (CTO): Thank you both.
[00:50:20] Mei (MLOps): Thanks.
[00:50:30] -- Meeting ends with scheduling logistics --

Notes on transcript quality: automated transcript had a few misrecognized product names (e.g., "token_guard" sometimes transcribed as "toner guard"), and occasional speaker label swaps. The above transcript has been lightly cleaned but preserves the conversational flow and some stutters.
